headings.title: Introduction to Basic Life Support (BLS)
headings.content: Basic Life Support (BLS) forms the foundational framework for saving lives during critical medical emergencies such as cardiac arrest, stroke, and severe airway obstruction. As nursing students in Nigeria, mastering BLS is vital because you will often be the first healthcare professionals to encounter these acute crises, both in hospital settings and within community outreach programs. BLS involves recognizing life-threatening emergencies, activating the emergency response system, performing high-quality chest compressions, delivering effective rescue breaths, and utilizing an Automated External Defibrillator (AED) without delay. Unlike Advanced Cardiac Life Support (ACLS), BLS focuses purely on non-invasive interventions and can be initiated by anyone, though healthcare providers must execute these skills with clinical precision. Prompt initiation of BLS maintains a critical flow of oxygenated blood to the brain and vital organs, drastically improving the chances of survival and reducing permanent neurological damage before advanced medical help arrives. Understanding these core principles equips you to act decisively and confidently when every second counts.

headings.title: The Chain of Survival in BLS
headings.content: The Chain of Survival is a standardized, sequential series of life-saving steps designed to maximize survival rates from sudden cardiac arrest. For adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, the links include immediate recognition of cardiac arrest and activation of the emergency response system, early CPR with an emphasis on chest compressions, rapid defibrillation with an AED, effective advanced life support, and integrated post-cardiac arrest care. In resource-limited settings across Nigeria, community awareness and early activation are paramount because transit times to advanced facilities can be prolonged. Each link in the chain is interdependent; if any link is weak or delayed, the overall chance of survival diminishes significantly. Healthcare providers must understand both out-of-hospital and in-hospital chains of survival, as the entry points differ slightly. In a hospital setting, the chain often begins with surveillance and prevention by vigilant nursing staff to identify deteriorating patients before a full cardiac arrest occurs. Recognizing your role within this integrated chain empowers you to coordinate rapid responses and bridge the gap between basic interventions and advanced medical care.

headings.title: Scene Safety and Assessment
headings.content: Scene safety and rapid assessment are the absolute first priorities for any nurse responding to an emergency. Before approaching a victim, you must scan the environment for potential hazards such as live electrical wires, traffic, fire, toxic gases, or violent bystanders, ensuring that you do not become another casualty. Once the scene is deemed safe, you quickly assess the victim by tapping their shoulder and shouting loudly to check for responsiveness. Simultaneously, look at the chest for normal breathing or signs of agonal gasps, which are not effective breathing and indicate cardiac arrest. This assessment should take no longer than 10 seconds to avoid delaying life-saving interventions. If the victim is unresponsive and not breathing normally, you immediately activate the local emergency response system (or instruct a specific bystander to call for help) and retrieve an AED if one is nearby. Practicing systematic scene safety and rapid assessment ensures an organized, efficient rescue process that protects both the rescuer and the patient.

headings.title: High-Quality Chest Compressions
headings.content: High-quality chest compressions are the single most critical component of effective Basic Life Support. To perform them correctly on an adult, place the heel of one hand on the center of the victim's chest (lower half of the sternum) and put your other hand on top, interlocking your fingers. Position your shoulders directly over your hands with your elbows completely locked straight, using your upper body weight to compress the chest. For adults, push hard and fast, achieving a depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) but no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm), at a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute. Crucially, you must allow complete chest recoil after every compression to allow the heart to refill with blood before the next stroke. Minimize interruptions in chest compressions, keeping pauses to less than 10 seconds during tasks like rhythm checks or ventilation. High-quality compressions generate artificial circulation, maintaining minimal perfusion to the brain and myocardium until normal heart rhythm is restored.

headings.title: Airway Management and Rescue Breaths
headings.content: Airway management and rescue breaths work in tandem with chest compressions to supply oxygen to the victim's body. To open the airway of an unresponsive adult without suspected spinal injury, use the head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver; if spinal injury is suspected, use the jaw-thrust maneuver instead. Once the airway is open, deliver rescue breaths using barrier devices like pocket masks or bag-valve-mask (BVM) systems to maintain infection control and optimal oxygen delivery. For conventional CPR in adults, the compression-to-ventilation ratio is 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Each rescue breath should be delivered over approximately one second, just enough to make the chest visibly rise. Avoid excessive ventilation, as over-inflation increases intrathoracic pressure, reduces venous return to the heart, and ultimately lowers overall survival rates. Effective coordination of compressions and breaths ensures a balanced delivery of oxygen and blood flow throughout the resuscitation effort.

headings.title: Automated External Defibrillator (AED) Operation
headings.content: An Automated External Defibrillator (AED) is a computerized, portable device capable of analyzing a victim's heart rhythm, identifying shockable rhythms like ventricular fibrillation (VF) or pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT), and delivering an electrical shock to restore a normal rhythm. When an AED becomes available, turn it on immediately and follow the clear audio and visual prompts provided by the device. Expose the victim's bare chest, wipe it dry if necessary, and apply the adhesive electrode pads correctly—typically one on the upper right chest and the other on the lower left side. While the AED analyzes the heart rhythm, ensure that no one touches the victim to avoid interference or accidental shock. If a shock is advised, the device will prompt you to clear the patient and press the shock button. Immediately resume high-quality chest compressions starting with compressions right after the shock is delivered. AED operation is straightforward and empowers even novice rescuers to successfully treat lethal cardiac arrhythmias.

headings.title: Managing Foreign-Body Airway Obstruction (Choking)
headings.content: Foreign-body airway obstruction (choking) can cause rapid asphyxiation if not promptly relieved. When dealing with a conscious adult or child suffering from severe choking—indicated by an inability to speak, cough, or breathe, often clutching the neck—you must immediately perform abdominal thrusts (the Heimlich maneuver). Stand behind the victim, wrap your arms around their waist, make a fist with one hand, place it just above the navel and well below the breastbone, and grasp your fist with your other hand. Pull inward and upward with sharp, forceful thrusts to increase intrathoracic pressure and force the trapped object out. Continue these thrusts until the object is expelled or the victim becomes unresponsive. If the choking victim becomes unconscious, gently lower them to the ground, activate the emergency response system, and begin CPR starting with chest compressions, checking the mouth for the foreign object before giving rescue breaths. Quick recognition and action can successfully clear airway blockages and save a life.

headings.title: Special Considerations and Post-Resuscitation Care
headings.content: Special considerations in BLS involve adapting techniques for unique populations such as pregnant women, infants, and victims of drowning, as well as understanding the fundamentals of post-resuscitation care. For pregnant victims in cardiac arrest, manual left uterine displacement is crucial during chest compressions to relieve aortocaval compression by the gravid uterus and improve venous return. For infants under one year, BLS involves using two fingers for compressions (or two thumbs-encircling hands if two rescuers are present) and delivering back blows and chest thrusts for choking instead of abdominal thrusts. Once spontaneous circulation is successfully restored (ROTC), post-resuscitation care focuses on maintaining adequate oxygenation, blood pressure control, targeted temperature management, and preparing the patient for advanced critical care transfer. As nursing students, knowing these modifications ensures safe and effective care across diverse clinical scenarios and promotes optimal recovery outcomes for patients.
